utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, together with Crispian Smith and, this morning, Jim Cruess, who's an intern.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mico Stanisic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Tatjana Savic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And unless there is some reason to -- Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Just one matter, Your Honour. These may be famous last words, but it appears this witness will finish early this week. It appears the parties have overestimated the time for his testimony; we estimated 8 hours for examination-in-chief, we only took five. All right. Only took five. Just under five. Monday evening the Prosecutor advised us that they would need six.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... no, four.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, by e-mail -- by e-mail on Monday evening we were told six, but be that as it may, it appears he'll finish early. To answer the question you had yesterday, Your Honour, we do not have another witness available for this week. I just want to repeat Mr. Zecevic's request to address you tomorrow on procedural and scheduling matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. Would the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just say something about this. I appreciate that it's not always easy to give estimates. This one was particularly over for the Defence and this witness. But my concern is this, I did say to Mr. Zecevic last week that it was highly unlikely that the witness would take the whole week. He did say that he only had the next witness lined up for Tuesday. And my concern is, given that we're told that other matters that Your Honours are going to be involved in will be starting at some stage, probably before the recess, that we shouldn't lose days unnecessarily. And in one sense it would be better to have a witness ready and available to go even if the witness maybe has to wait. But, I mean, that's the only thing I'm saying, because it seems to me that we have the possibility of losing a great deal of time over the next few months, potentially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, it's not an easy problem, but we're -- it -- and as you would be well aware, Ms. Korner, VWS has -- has views on this matter of having witnesses standing by, and it's something which is not easily resolvable. And it isn't peculiar to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I appreciate that. But, I mean, all I'm saying is this particular case the Defence were told that this witness was not going to take that long. In any event, having seen him yesterday, unless he's prepared to answer questions more shortly, he may well trickle into tomorrow morning, so that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Orasanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't realise you didn't have your headphones on. Yes, before Ms. Korner continues, I remind you you're still on your oath. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, yesterday His Honour Judge Delvoie pointed out that I asked you a question about Novo Sarajevo and whether Mico Stanisic had put out a statement saying that the attack had been carried out by what he described as Green Berets. And His Honour Judge Delvoie pointed out rightly that you went into a long description, and this is at page 21983, of what had actually happened and never answered the question I actually asked. Now, before I ask the question again, can I please ask you this morning - I think you would like to go home, and we would all like to be able to finish the cross-examination - just to answer the questions I ask. If I want more detail, then I will ask for it. Or if Defence counsel think that more detail is required, they can deal with it in re-examination. So do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the question I asked was: Did Mico Stanisic put out a statement to the effect that the attack had been carried out by Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is this: I know that it was the Green Beret that carried out the attack. I know it personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, that's what I mean. Just concentrate on the question, not what you know, say you know. The question was: Are you aware that Mico Stanisic put out a statement in which he said this was an attack by the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any such statement. However, I know that the Green Berets carried out the attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it's not on my list, but, in fact, Your Honours have already seen that. It's Exhibit P537. And I don't know whether Your Honours want me to call it up so that you can just see it. As the witness says, he didn't -- he doesn't know about that. I had it a minute ago. Can we just -- just call it up, if we could, just so you can see it because it came in a long time ago. 537. It's dated the 5th of April. I think it came in through Dr. Nielsen, such a low number. And you will see on the 3rd page -- second page you'll see the description of the attack in English. I think it's still the same page in B/C/S. "Novo Sarajevo Public Security Station was captured in a classic terrorist attack by so-called Green Berets." And can we go to the next page in B/C/S and the last page, third page, in -- you'll see there Mico Stanisic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you recognise, while we're on this document, Mr. Orasanin, is that Mico Stanisic's signature?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can we just for a moment go back to the description of your career that you gave yesterday. You told Mr. Cvijetic about your various appointments in the MUP. And that's at -- yes, you worked -- you told him, at page 21842, that you completed the police academy and so on and so forth. Then you went to the crime prevention department as chief in Novo Sarajevo until 1992. Then you worked as the crime prevention inspector, as you said, until November, when you went to border affairs, and then you told us that you became the deputy chief of public security in Zvornik until you retired.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: However, can you have a look, please, now at 65 ter 20151, tab 9, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a document -- in fact, it comes from Prijedor, Simo Drljaca, who was passing on information about appointments in 1994, and at number 14, do we see you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under 14 I can see the name Milomir Orasanin, chief of department for general crime prevention. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that's a document -- I don't understand. I have to see -- I have to look ... I was the chief of the public security station in Sarajevo in charge of general crime before the war, but that was in Novo Sarajevo. I had nothing to do with Prijedor at all. I'm analysing all the names.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, sorry. It's my fault. The copy of this document came from Prijedor, that's all I'm saying. That's why you see at the bottom that it's got Simo Drljaca's name. But this apparently is appointments which were made in 1994 when Mico Stanisic returned as minister of the interior, and I'm simply asking whether you were then, by him, made the chief of the department for general crime prevention? Is that so difficult, Mr. Orasanin? Surely you remember whether you were promoted.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked in the crime prevention department administration as an inspector in 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In November I joined the border affairs administration and there I was the chief of the department for border affairs. This may be a mistake of some sort.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you saying that this document, in showing you as being the chief of department for general crime prevention, is in error?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did do that previously, but at that time I was the chief of the department for border affairs, not for general crime prevention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, according to this list of May 1994, the chief of the department for border affairs is somebody called Slobodan Govedarica, at number 17.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a reshuffle, a new organisation was put in place, and there were times when border affairs was part of the general police and there were times when it was a special department. And there was a department for border affairs with its chief and there was also a section for border affairs, and its parts were public security stations in Zvornik, Bijeljina, and so on. This is what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Orasanin, this is really a simple question. Were you or were you not in 1994 made chief of the department for general crime prevention? The answer is either yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe that was part of a plan. I can't remember now, but I know I was assigned as the chief of department for border affairs. They are different organisations. Ministers changed every two years. And every time a new minister came, the first thing they did, they re-organised everything. The border affairs administration was at time merged with the police administration and there were also times when the border affairs administration was on its own, hence all the confusion and changes. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But -- all right. So you can't say yes or no; you can't remember. Are you saying you don't remember what was clearly a promotion?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I sit here, and I can say that in 1993 I worked, and in 1994 I was the chief of either the section or the department for border affairs. The titles changed. And police stations from Zvornik to Brcko were integral parts of that department. I don't see this as a promotion at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because all I was going to suggest to you, Mr. Orasanin, was that clearly Mico Stanisic thought very highly of your abilities as a police officer and promoted you in 1994. Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, let me put it this way, let me tell you the truth, I can't remember. Maybe that was planned. But my office was elsewhere from August. I had an office in Bijeljina and another one in Zvornik because of -- precisely because of this. I know I was told, You're going to take over everything regarding border affairs. But it was not only Mico Stanisic. Others thought that I was an honourable man, that I was a professional, and they told me, Choose an office where you will. It may be in Bijeljina or Zvornik, but things have to work. You have to surround yourself with professionals. I remember that. And I think that Tomo Kovac at one point when he joined, he also had the same opinion. I believe that the minister planned for that to happen. But within the next five days, I don't know what happened, because it is the assistant minsters in charge of various administrations who have the final say, and I agree that Mico Stanisic had a high opinion of me, but not only him, everybody else did. And vice-versa. I thought that he was the only professional minister that was in office. He was one of the first ministers, and I thought this it was my moral obligation to come here and to say what I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Now, can we just deal with some of the other names just to see whether this document is not what it purports to be. Did Tomo Kovac become the acting head of the public security department and an assistant minister in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a period of time when there were two different sectors, public security and state security. I don't remember when, whether that was in 1993 or 1994. You would have to jog my memory. And, yes, the answer is yes. Yes, he was. Yes, he was. There was the minister and his office composed of two different services, state security service, public security service; that was the organisation that was in place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Honestly, Mr. Orasanin, all I'm asking you is whether that's right. You don't have to give me a full explanation. As I say, if I need more explanation, I'll ask for it. Now, did an Andrija Bjelosevic become the -- be promoted from head of the CSB Doboj to assistant in the public security department at the headquarters? Either yes or no or you don't know.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here yes, but I don't remember that. I don't remember for how long was -- I'm reading the document, and it says so in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Now I'm asking you from your own knowledge because I want to see about this document. Did Vladimir Tutus, who you know, also become an assistant in the public security department?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says so here, but I remember him from a period after the war when he was one of the officials, but that was in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you remember Jesuric, who you knew, who had been in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he become the chief of administration for border affairs and foreigners?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the administration that I just mentioned a little while ago. This is part of that new organisation that was to be put in place. And pursuant to that there would have been a professional service for border affairs which had its lower-ranking units sections and police security stations, and Predrag Jesuric was the chief of that administration, whereas I was the chief of one of the departments.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I am going to ask that this be admitted and marked, please. It wasn't on our 65 ter list. Its relevance wasn't particularly apparent until this witness started to give evidence. I say straightaway, it's not just a question of the credibility of this witness, it also does go to the case because it shows, as you can see, other names having been promoted by Mico Stanisic in 1994. But we say it is relevant and admissible and the witness has been able to speak to it, even though he says he can't remember whether he got this promotion or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, this is a period beyond the scope of the indictment, so this is not relevant. It was not on the 65 ter list and it does not meet the requirements from the Prlic decision and we object.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We suggest it is 1994 but it's not the date that matters. It's the -- as I say, firstly, this witness's promotion, even though he says he can't remember, and other people who Your Honours have heard about or seen also apparently being promoted. That's the relevance. The fact that it's 1994, I agree is outside the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber is not persuaded that this document should be admitted into evidence. It is outside of the -- it is well outside of the relevant period, although promotions by their nature admittedly reflect what would have happened in the past, but this is well beyond the period. And also we have the witness's viva voce testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to just ask you, please, to deal for a moment with the Law on Internal Affairs that was promulgated in March of 1992. That is the law under which all members of the MUP acted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you have a look, please, on the screen, then, please, at a couple of sections. P530, and it's at tab 1B.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, at Article 28 first of all, which is, sorry, on the - one, two, three - fourth page in English and fourth page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that sets out the new CSBs that were going to be operating within the Serbian Republic. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have the Serbian version here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Article 28.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 28. I can only see Articles 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I said page 4, please, in B/C/S. And page 4, please, in English. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you were aware of that at the time, weren't you, that the -- instead of being -- you said there were eight CSBs under the old BiH MUP, in fact there were nine, but you agree that they were reduced to those five; you knew that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I spoke yesterday, I was referring to the old organisation of the former MUP, and then I listed the CSBs, Banja Luka, Doboj, Tuzla --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't list them again. Sorry, I shouldn't have mentioned you said there were eight under BiH, in fact we know, so you needn't worry about it, there were nine. But don't worry about that. Please just concentrate on this: Were you aware at the time in 1992, when you went back to the -- when you went to the new MUP, the Serbian MUP, that there were five CSBs?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was speaking about the stations in the eastern part of Republika Srpska. When we went there, they didn't belong to the Sarajevo CSB until the new organisation was set up. Later on they were placed under the Sarajevo CSB, and Zoran Cvijetic was chief. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to come on to what you say. All I'm asking you, Mr. Orasanin, please, concentrate on the question: Were you aware, when you started work at the MUP, as you say, the beginning of May, that there were five CSBs?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly knew that there was a CSB in Banja Luka, one in Doboj, then there were the undefined municipalities, and there was Trebinje. As I said, there were Bijeljina, Zvornik, Foca, Visegrad, they had an undefined status; and Foca, Visegrad, Rudo became parts of the Trebinje CSB. And there was a dilemma about Zvornik, as far as I know, and Bijeljina. And that's why a new centre was established in Bijeljina. There was a dilemma to who Zvornik should belong, whether to Bijeljina or to Sarajevo. When we went to the field, that was a problem for us because we didn't know who these stations belonged to. I said that they had been left hanging, to my understanding. And the SJBs in the eastern part, it was decided that, probably it was the minister who decided that, that they should become integral parts of the organisational structure of the MUP but that they should be placed under the Sarajevo CSB. That's what I know, and that was the basic problem, because you didn't know who to task to implement the obligations and authority under the Law on Internal Affairs. We were the ones who went to visit them first, and that was an ad hoc visit. That's what I said, that we didn't do what we were supposed to do. When we had made a snap-shot of the situation and we saw chaos, we wanted the people to act as police officers, but they weren't under our administration. They were uniform police and we were from the crime police department, but they were actually appointed by the local authorities. And that's why we sent other teams there too, because our idea when we set out from Pale was something else, but then we saw that there was chaos. There were people without appointments, and that's why we went about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, are you still answering the question whether you knew or not that there were five CSBs? Because I'm lost. Would you please -- would you please answer the question: Did you know that there were five CSBs or did you not know that at the time? Or did you know at the time there were more than five? That's a yes or a no or there were more. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I knew, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- during the period after our return in July, not when I went on my first visit. When I first went there to those SJBs in the east, I didn't know. And, in fact, there weren't, actually, because they didn't know who they belonged to. And we were there in the field and we made a snap-shot of the situation. And that's certain. That was the real state of affairs. And in May and June those stations did not belong to a centre. I'm positive about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So now it's clear: In May you did not know and people did not know because there was some uncertainty, but in July you did know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In late July.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Orasanin, I give you fair warning: Unless you answer my questions simply and in one sentence, you will be here not just today, but tomorrow and the day after. Now, is it your -- are you telling the Court that when you joined the MUP, you did not bother to look at the new Law on Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I was a member of the crime prevention administration, we were at different locations. There was a disorganisation. We were in one place, and the legal department was in a different place. In May I didn't know. Later I found out. Now I can't remember when the law was promulgated, and I must be honest, I accept what you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you seriously telling the Court, Mr. Orasanin, that as a professional, long-serving police officer you did not bother to look at the Gazette published in March which set out the new Law on Internal Affairs? Is that really what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in March I didn't know that. But I did know in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure if the witness said June or July.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you tell -- the interpreter wasn't sure whether you said June or July. I think that's because I left my mike on. When did you say you saw it, June or July?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose it was in June, because March 1992 was before the war, if we're talking about this period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Article 33, please, which should be on the same page in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which sets out the activities and tasks of the ministry and one of them is that it monitors, directs, and co-ordinates the activity of the Security Services Centre and public security stations. Is it under this provision that the inspections which were carried out by you and others took place?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I was saying that in 1992 it wasn't possible. We --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, don't you tell me, please, about the inspections. I'm going to come on to them. But I just want your agreement, and you have agreed, that it's under this provision that the inspections are carried out. Now, other than the inspection checklist, which I'm going to also come back with -- to, was there any other rule that specifically set down how inspections should be carried out?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a bylaw. But we also implemented the old laws and regulations that were taken over. So this instruction about instructional supervision was one from the former MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it's basically the same, and I remember those duties and obligations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. I fully accept that until later on in the year there was no new rule book. But what I want to know, please, is under what provision, apart from the Law on Internal Affairs, you carried out the inspections? Was it a -- was it in the rule book, was it somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was a bylaw, a piece of subordinate legislation, which was passed in 1993. It was called the instruction on instructive supervision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that. I know that there were new laws passed later on, but what I'm asking you is: As you were carrying over the old BiH rule book, was there any other provision in any old legislation, as you call it, which regulated the conduct of these inspections?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I remember there was this instruction. Or maybe it was called "the rule book on inspections." It was a bylaw.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, it's name may have been called "instruction on instructive supervision" or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those rules and bylaws and instructions are passed by the minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I fully accept that. What I want to know is, you mean there is a book that is headed "conduct of inspections" as issued by, the then minister it would have been, Delimustafic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in the former MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And you were using that when you carried out your inspections, were you, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we used that and applied it. We were duty-bound to do so. The inspectors who went out to conduct inspections must work by some rules where it is set out what they're supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you keep a copy of that rule book?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, before the war and in 1992, as I was saying, we didn't have a thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I fully understand you, you were using the old one. Do you -- what I mean is, do you still have in your possession a copy of that rule book?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was adopted in 1993, the crime prevention and detection administration, but that was later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, no. Do you have still, in your parents' place or wherever it is, a copy of the old BiH rule book on the conduct of inspections?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember. I know I did have a copy of the rule book about public security, but that's a thin booklet and little is said about this there. But in 1992 I did not have that rule book. But when we went out to do our work, we just worked from memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. All that I'm going to ask you to do, Mr. Orasanin, is to check, when you've finish testifying, to see if you have a copy of the book you were using in 1992 which sets out the guide-lines for inspections. And we'll deal with that at the end of your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, finally, can we look, please, at Article 41, which we will find on the sixth page in, I think, both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which sets out the special duties and powers of officials. And I want to go to the second column, please, the column on the right-hand side at the top where in the second paragraph it says: "The minister shall decide which employees will be considered authorised officials." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that is the provision, is it, that gives the minister the power to make appointments?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you have said yesterday, in answer to questions from Mr. Cvijetic, or maybe the day before, that unless there were written appointments made, none of the people could be considered to be -- none of the people who held positions, such as chiefs of the SJBs, could be considered to be members of the MUP. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was speaking about members of the service who didn't have appointments, that they couldn't exercise police authorities. And legally speaking they couldn't exercise police powers as laid down in the law if they didn't have appointments. That's why the appointments were temporary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that. And I'm going to come back to the actual reality in a little while. But what is there that prevents the minister making a verbal appointment rather than putting it into writing?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, firstly, before his appointment, that person must meet the general and the special conditions to be an employee of the MUP. And if he meets all these conditions, once he's appointed, can exercise police authorities, such as detaining persons, using force, including weapons, et cetera. That is that risk, to my understanding. That's why the appointments were temporary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I absolutely understand that. There are conditions laid down as to the qualifications that must be held. But what I'm simply asking you is: What is there to prevent the minister, particularly in a time of conflict and bad communications, from making a verbal appointment and not putting it into writing?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, and I may not be the most competent person to speak about this, but talking about the crime enforcement administration, there must be proposals and all the persons must be qualified and meet the general and special conditions to do that work. And of course, a certain time is required for that. You can't go about this hastily. You must check people, especially from some remote places. The procedure was rather slow, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What exactly -- and what I'm putting to you, Mr. Orasanin, is that in a time of conflict it is perfectly possible, in order to speed matters up, for the minister by telephone, or whatever it is, saying, You are appointed, even if only temporarily, as chief of the SJB, or whatever it may be. There's nothing that prevents that happening, is there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I must be honest and say what I know. My answer may not be correct. But at the stations that we visited in the eastern part, and I must stress that it is the eastern part, they were kind of hanging in the air, hovering. The local authorities were appointing people. Crisis Staffs, as I said, appointed commanders at Zvornik, Skelani, and other places, and that was a problem. The phone didn't even work. Traffic was disrupted, road traffic, I mean. There were technical problems and other problems. That's why the minister couldn't issue appointments, only temporary appointments. I think it would have been too much responsibility to authorise somebody over the phone to do something without applying the procedure and without checking people. The minister insisted on verified personnel that had experience from before the war. Goran Macar wasn't there, Dobro wasn't there, so I had to be present. He insisted that we find people, the old, experienced people. In other words, get rid of those lazy sods who only work for their personal gain. I remember that. And I brought an inspector, Cedo Tosic, who was appointed to a position in the police administration. Then there was Kapetanovic, Ratko Kapetanovic, who was in the crime prevention and detection administration. That was -- I worked on all that much more than on my proper line of business.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right, Mr. Orasanin, I don't want a full description of everybody you employed. I'm sticking to one simple principle. You said "the minister couldn't issue appointments, only temporary appointments. I think it would have been too much responsibility to appoint somebody over the phone ..." But that was his responsibility, wasn't it? because that's what the law said, the minister shall decide which employees will be considered authorised officials. And that's right, isn't it? And if you don't agree, say so. Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I disagree because --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... that's all you have to say.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the procedure wasn't applied. It was a huge risk, a huge responsibility, to appoint people who don't do their work and who aren't professionals. And then the minister is responsible for the activities of those people who are 100 or 200 kilometres away from the ministry headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to move on, please, to the evidence you gave on the day before yesterday, on Monday, when you were talking about starting work with the RS MUP, and you said -- or it was, in fact, when you were asked about the working conditions and you were shown the document which is a Defence document. It is, I think, 10D1, which is in the binder you have, or you no longer have but I'm sure the Defence will give it back to you. Tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Anybody want to give him his binder back?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were saying there was hardly anybody there, there was no phone, typewriters, or whatever. So this is right at the beginning or a month after the RS MUP has been put into place. And if we look at the first page, there are 16 people working at headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we go over to the next page in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's a further 24, isn't it, including a large number of communication officers? Eleven in all -- well, with the head, 12 in all. 24 people on that page. So working already in May are some 40 people in headquarters. Wouldn't you say that was at least an adequate number of people within a month of the MUP starting up?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to this document in terms of operative services, there's six plus four, a total of ten. And the rest are, auxiliary services. However, in the headquarters, in our headquarters, there was the police administration as well as the crime prevention department, and the two had a total of ten people; four or five in the administration for the police, and the other administration, four to five. We were in the headquarters Kalovita Brda. I don't remember where the communications centre was, maybe on Mount Jahorina. The administration for administrative affairs was also located somewhere, if my memory serves me, in a restaurant or in a hotel, also on Mount Jahorina, some 200 kilometres away. So this document was drafted in the administration for legal affairs. They had more modern typewriters, I can see. There were ten people in operative administrations. In the public security service, that is a public service that works pursuant to the law that we just saw a little while ago. The police administration, the crime prevention administration, a total of ten.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But look, at the headquarters, wherever they -- and I agree they were in separate buildings, part was in Vraca school in May, there were no less than 40 people working. That does not include, if you go through the document, because you were taken through it by Mr. Cvijetic on Monday, all the other people that we can see if you go to the next page in English and B/C/S. The specialist staff, over the page, crime investigation. All crossed out but you say that you don't understand the crossings-out because everybody was working there, and so on and so forth. So I'm suggesting to you, Mr. Orasanin, that to say that there were no personnel and no communications at this period is simply not right, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about May and the beginning of June. The roads were not passable towards public security stations in the eastern part.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not -- please, Mr. Orasanin, I'm not talking about how you got about. I'm talking about the number of staff that were working at the MUP headquarters in May, because this is a payment list for May. Anyhow, I've made my suggestion. Let's move on, please. Can you look, please, now at a document which is 20 -- 65 ter 20162. It's tab 4A, you haven't got it, Mr. Orasanin, of the Prosecution binder. Now, do you recognise this book, as we look at the cover?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Perhaps we can zoom in on the label. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just read out what it says?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: CSB, the Security Services Centre notebook or log-book. A log-book of staff, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, let's go to the next page, please. I think you'll find it's not that. In B/C/S. You can stay on the same page in English, thank you. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does that say "sent and received dispatches"?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And does that show, just to take the first example, 22nd to the 23rd of April from the minister of the interior, a daily events bulletin, which is going to those places that we can see listed in the next column?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We go, please, to item number -- we'll leave out the media stuff that follows, item number 4, 24th of April, from the Serbian MUP in S MUP BiH Vraca, as I say, part of the MUP was there. Does that show a decision going out, temporary assignment to the head of the SJB Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 24 April 1992, Vraca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we go into May, can we go, please, to -- well, actually, no, let's go to number 15, please, on this list. Still in April.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And 15 is on the fourth page of the document in English. No, in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a moment, if I may. This is a document which is not on a 65 ter list. The signatory in the column entitled "remark" was a Prosecution witness, however, he was not shown this document although he was a competent witness. I'm afraid that we are now showing a document to the witness who is not competent to talk about the communications system, or at least not as thoroughly as the -- as Witness Radovan Pejic. So this document does not meet the requirements that I mentioned a little while ago, primarily, it's not on 65 ter list. We will not get very far with this witness unless we read through everything that is written in here. However, whether this witness is going to be able to draw any valid conclusions based on this document, I'm not sure. I don't think that we will go very far with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the point that I'm obviously making is because of what the witness asserts about the lack of communication and the no staff and all the rest of it. As to -- this wasn't, I understand, on the 65 ter list. It was, however, disclosed to the Defence in 2008. [Microphone not activated] Sorry, Your Honours, I'm just checking on the history of this one. Your Honours, it appears it was added but withdrawn and we're having a slight problem in sorting it out. But the point is, I'm not seeking to exhibit it. I'm merely going through this with the witness to see if he'll agree that clearly what he's saying about communications cannot be, putting it at its lowest, entirely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I have a bit of a problem, Ms. Korner. Whereas I appreciate the -- that the witness is -- that you will elicit particular answers from the witness, the problem is that, this not being an exhibit, the -- it is -- he is, to my mind, being challenged as to the reliability, to put it at its lowest, of his answers against a document which is not before the Chamber. That's the disconnect that I'm having.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, well, that's the difficulty on Your Honours' ruling about this question of exhibits, is that things become much more relevant when we have a witness like this. And so documents which obviously have always had some relevance but not enough to try and get it on become much more relevant, and I would like to exhibit it. But, I mean, if Your Honours' ruling is that something which advances our case, although this one has actually been disclosed, and disclosed in 2008, we have difficulty in getting in, then I'm in a bit of a quandary, as it were. I understand what Your Honour says. I would, provided the witness, which actually -- I'm sorry, I'm interrupting my own train of thought. I should, of course, check that he's familiar with books like this and that he may recognise his signature. I'm sorry, I'm being told something else. Would Your Honours forgive me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can we -- Your Honours, I'm sorry, can I help. I have a feeling that we may have -- it is an exhibit already, after all of this. We're just going to check. I was quite surprised to hear it wasn't an exhibit when I saw the 20.000 number, but it seems to have a different 65 ter number. So can I be just given a minute or so, or shall I move on while we check this out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Perhaps that would be the better course, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. We'll come back to this, then. Your Honours, we're just doing a double-check. We -- the trouble is we have a number of versions, and sometimes we get the 65 ter numbers right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may we be of assistance as well. The document has been exhibited, and it was commented upon by a competent witness, as P1428. It was admitted during the examination of a witness who explained the essence of all of the documents listed in here. I believe that we shed enough light on this document with a competent witness. I don't think that we can advance any further with this witness. We can't do more than we did with the witness who is the signatory of this document, who was here and commented upon it when he testified in this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, if you are correct that the document is an exhibit, isn't it open to counsel to challenge the witness on the stand against the -- what that document shows if it is inconsistent with the representations which he has made so far? I take your point about it not being on the 65 ter list and he not being the author and whatnot, but you have an official document which is exhibited, as you say, and the -- Ms. Korner is cross-examining a witness who is testifying to the same facts which are contradicted, on the face of it, by the exhibit. So what's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... and it was on our 65 ter -- Your Honours, it was on our 65 ter list, and it's P1428. And I -- it's our fault but, nonetheless, I don't think Mr. Cvijetic has any further objection that he can possibly make.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me just say, the witness who testified here had worked and was in charge of the communications systems, and he explained in very great detail practically every entry in this document. I'm afraid that this witness is in no position to know any more about this document, so that's why I'm saying we cannot go any further with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We hear you, Mr. Cvijetic, but that's an argument, and we will no doubt come to it later. Yes, Ms. Korner, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not in any way seeking to get him to explain this book. I'm getting him -- I'm challenging his assertion that there was no communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, do I need to take you through any more of this document, Mr. Orasanin, or do you accept that your assertion of no staff and no communications simply isn't right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer your question. Actually, I already answered this question during our first visit in May. We didn't have a possibility to communicate. Whether dispatches were later on sent at the local level in terms of different frequencies, I'm not an expert. I'm not competent. The chief of communications was Dragan Tesanovic. He could answer your questions. And Pejic, Dragan was in Sarajevo. He was the head of our communications centre in Sarajevo, and they are privy to that part of communication. But I know that there was a report when we visited the police stations in Vogosca and Ilijas, people told us there that they could not communicate between Ilijas and Vogosca, therefore they could not co-operate, and the distance between the two was only about 20 to 30 kilometres. And this is what is imprinted in my mind, that the communications did not function. We could not report back from Skelani. I'm talking about the month of May. Now, if this could function at the local level, I don't know how it was possible because I don't know anything about communications. Maybe dispatches could be sent by some other lines of communication --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, all I am putting to you is - forget, please, about outside MUP headquarters - that as far as headquarters, wherever the buildings were, they had communication, they were able to send and receive documents. Now, do you accept that is correct, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may have been at a local level, I don't know. I have never seen this log-book before. I don't remember that we at the crime prevention administration used this. This is my answer. I don't know if their service could do something. We couldn't. I'm talking about the month of May and the beginning of June. As far as I know, it was only in late 1992 that communications were properly up and running. I have never seen this before, and I don't know anything about this. I don't know whether it was possible at a local level. I claim that there was no communication between these two public security stations and there were no dispatches sent, and that's what I was governed by in my previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Have a look, please -- that's all I'm going to ask you about that document. Have a look, please at document which is P1437.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Tab 5 of the Prosecution binders, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the daily reports, Mr. Orasanin?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not during this period. This is a bulletin of daily events, right, in public security stations? At least this is what I'm reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, this is sent by the -- if you look at the handwritten at the top --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we pull down the B/C/S slightly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does that read "sent at 2150 hours to the Serbian news agency and the government"?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a MUP headquarters daily report. In fact, it's number 12. So these were documents that you had seen before; is that right, or the type of document?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I didn't know that daily reports were sent to -- this is our internal document as far as I know, but I may be mistaken. You will allow me that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want to deal with two -- three matters. In the second paragraph, does that deal with what is happening in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the third paragraph, does that deal with what is happening in Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we go over the page, please, just in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the fourth paragraph, does that deal with what is happening in Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you focus --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we can highlight, please, the fourth paragraph in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You see Novo -- immediately after Ilijas, does it talk about Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Do you agree that somehow or other, regardless of the conditions, on the 4th of May MUP headquarters is able to get information about what is happening in those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this. I was not familiar with this during this particular period of time. I know nothing about Novo Sarajevo. I knew nothing about this. I'm not familiar with the document either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. The question was: Do you agree, from reading this document, that somehow MUP headquarters is able to get information from these places which you say had no communications?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the 4th of May, telephones were up and running in town. There was communication before that time. All communication lines were up and running during this period of time, I think. Later on there were disruptions, after the 4th of May. There were separations, as it were, and the communication lines were disrupted. And during this particular period of time I think that telephones were up and running. You could call from one station to a place in the city. There were no separation lines in the city, as far as I can remember, which means that you could establish communication during this period of time. You could make telephone conversations. I don't know about teleprinter communications; I don't know if that was disrupted at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, forgive me, Mr. Orasanin, I understood from your long non-answer to one of my earlier questions that there was no communications between Ilijas and Vogosca at this period. When do you say -- from what period do you say there was no communication?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven days after this period, something happened. This is the beginning of war. Before the war, all communication lines were up and running. The situation was normal. After the 4th of May when the war started, somebody else started controlling their communications system. I don't know how it was done. I'm not an expert. I don't know how that worked. Some ten days later, there were disruptions left, right, and centre. And it all depended on who controlled what, which part, which ... and as far as I remember, the chief was Kezunovic. He is an engineer, and he's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, don't you worry about Mr. Kezunovic. It is generally accepted that the conflict started around the -- between the 4th and the 6th of April, not the 4th of May. Now, you're saying, are you, it was only a week after the 4th of May, so roughly the 11th of May, that communications began to be disrupted? Is that what you're saying? A simple yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I misspoke. I meant the 4th of April. And, here, this information was issued on the 4th of May. That's why I said the 4th of May and that's why I said 10 or 15 days later everything was disrupted, when we were in Skelani, Brcko, Zvornik, during our first visit, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, that's the point I've been trying patiently, I hope, to make to you; that you clearly are wrong when you suggest that there was no communications going on in May between MUP headquarters and Ilijas and Vogosca. Do you accept that, having seen this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that there were no communications between Ilijas and Vogosca, because people there complained. They complained that they couldn't get in touch with the closest municipality. They complained to us. I would have forgotten that if there hadn't been this report. I know that there was always a problem that they couldn't communicate, that they couldn't call in, that the communication lines were down, that there were disruptions. I don't know what kind of disruptions there were, but I know that they could not send this information from Skelani or elsewhere. There were no telephones up and running. We could not -- ourselves, we could not call our own boss to report back to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's probably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the break now, to resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, I want to move to the topic of the inspections themselves. First of all, did you see reports on inspections that had been done by other inspectors as part of your job?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I remember, some. After our stay on 25 August, but I don't remember which ones exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. But obviously if you were inspecting somewhere which had previously been inspected by another inspector, you would want to check, would you not, to see what they had done, reported on?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case since we were the first team, there were no previous inspections. We were the first ones to go there, and after us I think that some other teams went there, after the 15th of May and the 25th of August, our visits to Doboj and Foca in early September.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in fact we'll see that the -- before you went to Doboj there had been an earlier inspection of Doboj, but I think you've dealt with the matter. Now, is it also correct that during the period of 1992 until you left in November, working in the administration for crime prevention and detection - you've dealt with Mr. Planojevic and Mr. Macar - were yourself, Inspector Milanovic.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Inspector Ostoja Minic.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And somebody called Inspector Sinisa Karan.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Sinisa Karan came to the administration later, possibly even after I left, but I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] All right. Now, you told us, or you told Mr. Cvijetic on Monday, when you were shown the inspection checklist, and this is at page 21870, that he put to you: "Could you tell us how many employees and from which services of the ministry would be involved in such an inspection?" And you said: "The document talks about the manner of work and inspection. For such work you would need two or three inspectors who would be able to examine the entire situation." Now, it's right, isn't it, that you, in fact, on these inspections always had at least two and sometimes three inspectors? Don't worry about the document. I'll tell you -- I'll come back to the document. I just want you to answer that question, please. It's right, isn't it, from what we've seen, there were at least two of you and at least sometimes three of you doing these inspections?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, two are sufficient for an inspection of one administration, that is, one region. But in other cases, three or more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But there were three of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So in fact, when you told Mr. Cvijetic that it needed at least two or three to do the job, you were able in every case to do the job properly, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was speaking about our first visit, that we had problems there because we had nothing to inspect there, as those police stations were not under our administration. Later there was Doboj --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, no, no. Sorry, I understand what you're saying. You say that in the earlier inspections there weren't any police stations to inspect, but you appear to give the impression that you weren't able to carry out the requirements on this checklist because you needed two to three people. But as I'm pointing out to you, you did have at least two and often three people to do these inspections. So you were able, when there was a police station that was operating, to carry out a proper inspection; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some towns, no. But in Doboj we were able to conduct an inspection. That's what I said when I gave my first statement in 2005, that we had problems on our first visit and the real -- the only one was in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Please don't just repeat everything over again. You were able, if a police station was functioning properly, to carry out the full inspection, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if it was functioning and if the management was under our command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you would always do a report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a rule to write a report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And you would give that report, would you, to your direct supervisor, Mr. Macar?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reports of a uniformed team of inspectors was submitted to Mr. Macar, my supervisor. But if it was a mixed team, including inspectors from the uniformed police, then reports would be submitted in accordance with the respective lines of work. That is, the inspector for the uniformed police would do these tasks, and the crime prevention inspector would deal with crime prevention matters. Everybody would inspect their line of work. That's in accordance with the rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. But the whole idea, wasn't it, was so that through the chain of command - that is, from inspectors to Mr. Macar to Mr. Planojevic - the minister, Mr. Stanisic, would be informed of any problems that were occurring in the places where you did inspections?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, if the conditions allowed that. But we didn't write a report after our first inspection because we were in a traffic accident. And the incident was suspicious because it may have been staged.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I appreciate that's what you are saying. I didn't want to jump ahead, but why did -- I understand you had the accident and you had some injuries, but what was to prevent you, after you had recovered from the accident, and your colleagues from using your notes to put in a report, even if it was a late report?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't write reports because this colleague was transferred to hospital and he stayed there for some 10 or 15 days and we were also injured, and basically I didn't even report to anybody at work for a while, maybe 10 days or so. And that is why we didn't write a report. And that was a very short visit to those stations. We didn't do much work because we simply couldn't. We were driven out of Brcko by sniper fire. If we had done anything, I probably wouldn't be here now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm sure it was a very distressing experience for you, Mr. Orasanin, but what I'm asking you is: Didn't Mr. Macar or Mr. Planojevic say to you, Now that you've recovered from this nasty experience, could we have a report, please, about what you found?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't submit a report. I don't know if Drago Borovcanin ever did that for his line of work, because the greater problem was with the police administration and their remit, since the police stations, that is, the uniformed police are far more numerous and they have specific tasks. So I don't know whether he submitted a report for his line of work, but I don't think so after our injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Orasanin. Now, if there were problems as identified in one of the inspection reports, it was the job, wasn't it, of the minister, through his subordinates, to deal with those problems, to put into place solutions; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about a later period, then, yes, I would agree. But in 1992 there was so much confusion. It was the phase of the organisation, the setting up of the service. The centres, the administrations, that was a problem. I said so in my first statement, that the ministry was only being set up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I know that, but who -- even if the ministry was only being set up and even if there was confusion, it was the job, wasn't it, of the minister to deal with the problems that arose?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that. We did the things that had to do with our administration and our tasks. What the relations were between minister and minister, well, I'm not privy to that. We did work in the field, and that's why we don't know what happened later, where that information went or our reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, when you say you don't know what happened later to your reports, you, for example, described how the minister had taken action over what was happening in Foca and other places. Wasn't it clear to you that the minister was getting the information?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Goran Macar issued me that order. He said to me, See about this and prepare our activities. That's what I remember. And I drafted something by hand, considering who was available in terms of human resources. I was -- I limited myself to the crime prevention department.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did anybody other than the minister have the power to issue an order removing or replacing the head of an SJB?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, under the law, it's the minister who appoints people; whereas the nominations come from the centres. These are the legal provisions, I think. That was after the centralisation of the MUP. The war broke out when the MUP was centralised, as compared to a pre-war situation when it was decentralised. In 1984 [Realtime transcript read in error "1994"] there was a decentralisation of the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry about the history, please. Did anybody other than the minister have the power to order --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, I believe that the year was wrongly recorded in line 17. It says "1994." I believe the witness said "1984." That's how it was interpreted. Ms. Korner must have heard it too. The reference to the pre-war decentralisation, the year is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, it's just been wrongly --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry, Mr. Orasanin, it's just been wrongly recorded. I heard through my earphones "1984," not "1994." Did anybody other than the minister have the power to order the reduction of reserve policemen? Yes or no, please. Not an explanation. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know as far as appointments go that in 1992 the centre chiefs were authorised to issue temporary appointments, but I'm not sure which centres those are. I'm referring to temporary appointments of police officers. And they also had the authority to downsize the reserve police. So centre chiefs were authorised to issue temporary appointments for police officers in police stations, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that's because Mico Stanisic delegated that authority to them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that they made decisions on these appointments, I mean the centre chiefs, but whether they were authorised to do so, I cannot remember. But that's not my line of business. We had information that the centre chief can appoint a person to do the work of a police officer in a police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, you told the Court on Monday, at page 21872, that your priorities - I'm trying to find it, 21872 - were staffing at the places you inspected and also the crime reports; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was saying that we were duty-bound to check what the crime prevention services of some SJBs were doing. We were inspecting the crimes log and everything else that had to do with crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, let's -- can we just take, please -- have another look at that inspection checklist.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which you've got at tab 34 in your binder, Mr. Orasanin. Defence binder. Now, if we look again at some of the items, you have to -- it says "purpose" -- it says: "In the course of the inspection of investigation departments, it is necessary to meet employees, working meeting," and then, "purpose of the inspection: Gain an insight into criminal charges submitted." That is in the KU log-book entries. And then the records, other records, including, and that's one before the bottom on the English, "the log-book of on-site investigations"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then over the page, please, in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Upon completion of the inspection, a written report is to be compiled ... positive qualities, failures noted ... and then submitted to" it makes it quite clear it has to go to the minister, the assistant minister, the CSB head, and the files. So that there's no question but that your report had to go to the minister, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Talking about this instruction, I was saying that in our report itself where it says visit to police stations, and I don't want to be very long again, that we didn't use the term "inspection" but "visit." And -- but if we choose the term "inspection," then what you said follows from that. But since it wasn't possible, there were no conditions on the occasion of our first visit, possibly with the exception of Doboj, the terms we used, visits to police stations. And we did some of what is listed here. In Doboj we had a meeting. It is logical to look at the rule book on internal organisation, if it's in effect, to see how many inspectors there are, what they do, the structure, and then start reviewing the log-books, such as the KU log-book and the others. It is logical that then a report must be submitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but whether you called it a visit because you couldn't, for the reasons you've explained, carry out a full inspection, nonetheless, the report that you made had to go, didn't it, to the same people because that was the purpose of the visit?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were duty-bound to submit a report to our supervisor and that was Goran Macar. He was the coordinator, or his official position was assistant minister of the interior, as far as I know. And before him it was Dobrislav Planojevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry about who it was before. All right. Let's consider the KU books. The purpose of that inspection, is that right, was to see whether there were any anomalies in the books?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose is to make a review in accordance with the checklist. But at the time we didn't have this checklist. We used the pre-war checklist. So we worked based on our experience from before the war. And by inertia we went about this job, and what we saw there we also recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, stop, please, Mr. Orasanin. That's not the question I asked. But you've now sent me down another side track. Even if this list was produced during 1992, is there any difference between this list and the previous list that you had?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Was there any difference between the old checklist that came from the BiH MUP, the joint MUP, and this one?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is more or less the same, that it contains the same duties for the crime prevention department. Or at least that's how it should be. I cannot be very precise now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, when you were -- let's go back to my original question. When you were checking the KU books, was one of the purposes of doing it to see whether there were any obvious anomalies; for example, that there were too many unknown perpetrators being listed?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember that when we were in Doboj that we reviewed --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- I want the general principle, please. As a general principle, with your years of experience, when you were checking the books, was one of the purposes to look for anomalies, things that weren't right, based on your experience?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The KU log-book contains the reported crimes, with the dates and so on, as well as the subsequent activities where that criminal report ended up --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We know what the KU books contain. We've got the KU books. What I'm asking you is what was the purpose of your inspecting them. Was it to look for things that suggested were not quite right in what was happening?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the purpose was to identify any shortcomings and whether they worked in accordance with the procedure when it comes to reported crimes. Where those criminal reports ended up, whether they were submitted to the prosecutor's office, because that was their duty under the Law on Criminal Procedure. And then the prosecutor's office should trigger a further work to clarify those --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop. I don't want to deal with that. One of the things you would be looking for is to see whether they had put in criminal reports to the prosecutor's office; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what we required. I said that this inspection was done in Doboj. And as far as Skelani, the others, are concerned, well, there were -- those were very short visits because the service wasn't really organised, but in Doboj, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you understand what is meant by "general principles," Mr. Orasanin?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: General principles follow from a rule, from an attitude or from the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I'm not asking you specifically what you found at the moment in Doboj or Skelani or anywhere. I'm just asking you what, as an experienced inspector, you were looking for when you inspected the KU books. And you've said already to see whether reports were being sent to the prosecutor. Would a book full of reported crimes with a lot of unknown perpetrators be something that you would query?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, we wanted to see the results of the crime prevention department's activities. We wanted to see what they did under the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, no. Right, because -- I'm sorry, is the answer to my question, which I will repeat, would a book full of reported crimes with a large number of unknown perpetrators be something that you would raise with either the chief of the SJB or the CSB or the relevant official at the place you were inspecting?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, we would take stock of the numbers and we would see what activities had been undertaken. That's what we did. We spotted problems and we insisted on task forces to be established in order to deal with the problem. That was our obligation under the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll try one more time, Mr. Orasanin. Concentrate hard. If you saw a KU book that was full of crimes with unknown perpetrators recorded, would that be something that you would raise with the officials at the place that you were inspecting?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was our analytical service that did that. They looked at the reports. It would be the head of the department for crime prevention and the police department who did that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether when you saw it, you personally, you would think that was something that should be reported, something you should raise with -- you personally, with the officials at the place you were inspecting?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that the question has been asked and answered. He even gave you a very concrete example as to what was done in situations when there was a large number of criminal reports featuring unknown perpetrators in Doboj.
