I believe that the question has been asked and answered in a very concrete manner. The witness did say what they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I disagree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I was about to say, Mr. Cvijetic, in my view the question has been asked several times. I'm not sure it's been answered directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I'll try it one last time, Mr. Orasanin. When you saw a book -- and, all right, let's say, for example, as in Doboj, with a large number of unknown perpetrators, is that something you would raise at the time? You, not your analytical section.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we discussed that at our meetings and we launched initiatives for task forces to be set up in order to deal with that. And then in our subsequent visits, we would have looked at the results of our previous remarks. So as a result of our first visit, we established how many unknown perpetrators there were. And then we set up operative groups in order to elucidate those crimes. I remember that we wrote a report to that effect. And then during the subsequent visit, the one that I wasn't a part of, they went there to see what concrete results had been achieved, they visited all the other centres, they wanted to see what activities had been undertaken and involved the chief of the centre. Of course, it's logical, and that was our obligation. And information on all of that would have been contained in our reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Exactly. And what applied to Doboj applied everywhere else as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And indeed it was important enough, as you say, for the information to go to your analytical section; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We submitted reports to the crime prevention administration. If a team was mixed, then it -- the reports would go to both administrations, the police administration and the crime prevention administration. And then the respective heads contacted our head of service, not us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. All right. [Indiscernible]. In 1992, when you were going to areas where you knew that there had been conflict, would the fact that nearly all reports appeared to be against non-Serbs in any way cause you to ask questions at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that our visit to the stations in Skelani, Zvornik, and Brcko was a blitz visit and that we couldn't do much there, practically nothing. For example, in Zvornik the station had not even been set up, there was no chief --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. When you were doing your visits outside that first one that you've told us about - and, for example, let's take Doboj again - was the fact that the whole crime register appear to mainly have reports against non-Serbs something that caused you to question what was happening?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. But in Doboj, when we looked at the crimes, there were some known perpetrators, there were some murders or killings, for example, a Serb killed another Serb, and there were victims on both sides, both Serbs and Bosniaks. The reports that we analysed prompted us to launch an initiative to elucidate all of those crimes. I remember that. Irrespective of who the victims were, we formed operative groups that would collect information, and so on and so forth. It was not our obligation to contact any of the courts or the prosecutor's offices. We still contacted them. We were the ones behind the initiative to get both of them involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Look, look, all I'm asking, Mr. Orasanin, is this: Whether if you saw that there appeared to be an overwhelming preponderance of reports against non-Serb perpetrators, would that be something that you would ask questions about? Either yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We spoke to the crime prevention service again and we asked them to work on all of the cases, all 11 of them, and then the inspectors were resent out to see what had been done in the meantime, from the first to the second visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the 11 cases that had unknown perpetrators. Now, for the last time, Mr. Orasanin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, could you eventually ask the witness whether he noticed the fact you're putting to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm trying to get general principles.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you noticed, when you were checking the KU book, that the overwhelming number of cases had non-Serb perpetrators, not unknown ones, named non-Serb, would you have raised that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only talk about what I know, about the 11 cases. Those were war crimes, as far as I could see, as far as I could glean from the reports, if we are talking about those 11 cases that were crimes, that were homicides. And in legal terms and in logical terms that was what it was, and we were behind the initiative to set up teams that would deal with those cases. That's why we sent reports, Madam Prosecutor. This is my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. This is actually the last time. Leave aside Doboj and the 11 cases, please. If when you conducted inspections in places that had KU books and you noticed that in those books the overwhelming majority of crimes had non-Serb perpetrators, is that something you would have queried at the time? Please, either yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can -- I really apologise, I can only tell you what I know, what I saw with my own two eyes on my inspection visits to those stations. And if we're talking about rules and regulations, then yes. However, what I noticed, what I observed, is what I told you and what was entered in the reports about those stations. I'm talking about things that we were looking for. We looked at all the criminal reports and we insisted on the law being observed and carried out. That was our obligation. That was our task. If we're talking about general rules, they arose from rules and regulations and from the laws. I am telling you what I saw, what I was in a position to see. And I'm just sharing with you what my mental capacities allowed me to see at the time. There were no conditions in place for us to do full inspection supervision. I'm always coming back to the inspection supervision. It is a very tall order, in legal terms, to do an inspection supervision. I'm just sharing with you what I saw, what we observed, and what our obligation was. And all the police forces do that. It's not something that only we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'll ask the simple question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I take it that at line -- at page 48, line 2, at the end of line 2, the witness answered your hypothetical question. But it's still a hypothetical question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not, Your Honour, with respect. I'm going to ask the specific question that Your Honour wanted me to ask, because it's not hypothetical, it's what he considered to be part of his job, with his experience. So it's not a hypothetical question, but I will ask the specific question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'm sorry that I was trying to get general principles, unsuccessfully.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you went to Doboj on what was a proper, full, complete inspection that took two days, did you notice in the KU book for Doboj that the majority of named perpetrators were of non-Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. I don't understand your question. What do you mean by perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The word "perpetrator" in Serbian was used, the non-Serbian perpetrators. Can you repeat?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Croatian variant of the word was used and that -- the interpreter believes that that may be the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, we've been using "perpetrators" throughout the whole case without anybody telling us you can't call them perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: People accused of crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, do you now understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not sufficiently. When we looked at the KU, the question was whether we noticed the list of Serbian perpetrators of crimes or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, stop. I'll repeat the question again, as the translation went haywire. When you inspected the Doboj KU book in August of 1992, did you notice that the bulk of people accused of crimes were of non-Serb ethnicity, Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. There were some crimes committed by known perpetrators, both Serbs and Bosniaks. As far as I can remember, there were several such cases. And there were also crimes committed by unknown perpetrators. It was our obligation to look at the crimes committed by unknown perpetrators, those crimes that hadn't been elucidated by then. And we urged them to collect information and to submit that information to the prosecutor's office. And I remember that there were two Serb cousins who were both the perpetrator and the victim of a crime and the criminal report had been filed. So there were all sorts of different things there. Maybe if you showed me the document again, you would jog my memory, but that's -- this is my answer to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, show you what document again?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were to see that document or those documents, those criminal reports featuring unknown perpetrators of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about unknown perpetrators. I'm talking about allegedly known perpetrators. Do you understand the question, Mr. Planojevic -- Mr. Orasanin? When you looked at the KU book in Doboj, which you say you did, did you notice the vast majority of those persons accused of crime were non-Serb? If you didn't, then say so.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice that. Maybe it was the next team that noticed that, but I really can't remember. And I'm being sincere when I say this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, finally, before I look at some of the inspections that you did, you told us you didn't file a report in the respect of your first visit, I'll call it, but did you give a verbal report to Mr. Macar or Mr. Planojevic about what you found there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about my first visit, as far as I can remember, Macar was not my superior. We had been sent on that first visit by Cedo Kljajic, who was the chief for public security at the time, and our team was a mixed team consisting of Drago Borovcanin on behalf of the uniformed police, myself, and Pekic, Petko Pekic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If it was Mr. Kljajic, did you give a verbal report of what you pound to anybody at headquarters, when you finally got back there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered your question. We had that incident and the short break and my colleague was in hospital and for a while I was in a village and we didn't file any reports. We didn't submit reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I know you didn't file a written report. I hope the translation's not going wrong here. Did you speak to Mr. Kljajic or anybody else and say, Look, this is the problem that we've found in Skelani or Zvornik or whatever it is?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because after the incident I joined the crime service, and I did not see Cedo Kljajic for a month or maybe two. His office was in Vraca and my office was in Kalovita Brda. So after our visit and our return, I really didn't see him. I reported to Kalovita Brda, in Pale, and his office was not in Pale but in Vraca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, are you saying that your bosses, the senior officials in the MUP who sent you off on this visit or inspection, whatever you call it, that nobody, none of them, asked you, and not you personally, or any of your colleagues what you had found? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that. That was the organisation in place. It was the early days. Drago Borovcanin, I believe, along his line which was uniformed police, it is possible that he conveyed some information, because he was the least wounded of all of us in that incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's all I wanted to know. Thank you. Now, the inspection of Zvornik that you did - let's deal with these places - you did that in about mid-May; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you have a look, please, then, at the document which is 1C in the Prosecution tab, which is -- it's got a number 20160.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's not 1C.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Oh, we did have -- that's right, it was the -- sorry, it's P346. I've forgotten that we had discovered that it had been admitted as well. P346.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I don't know -- well, you may have seen this before. Have you ever seen this before?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But this is the report that they sent you -- sorry, sent you -- sent to the CSB at Bijeljina about what they had done between April the 1st and the 30th of June, and this is the station you say wasn't working at all and indeed you could only go to, I think you said Karakaj or something like that. During this period, 300 individuals were interviewed, 200 statements --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, page 2 in English and page 2 in B/C/S. No, page 1. Sorry, page 1 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 300 individuals were interviewed, 200 statements taken about the activities of Muslims, 80 searches of apartments and other premises belonging to Muslim extremists, all police station employees armed but lack of communications equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if we go to the third page in English and I think it's the second page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In addition to that, the employees, the crime prevention department were engaged in operative tasks. At first when the conflict broke out, there were three inspectors, later on an additional five inspectors were hired and a chief of the crime prevention department appointed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Please the next page in English. Same page in B/C/S, I think. Sorry, no, can we go to page -- sorry, we should be on page 2 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does that say "tasks and activities of the police station" in B/C/S? In the middle of the --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Underneath that, in English, "Zvornik public security service currently employs," and nobody can read it because something's gone over it, "members of the police, 33 are active police officers, all management posts have been filled."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go down the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "In the reporting period, the police employees brought in 537 persons for interview and interviewed 48 Muslim extremists."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "There were 336 inspection outings on the territory of the Zvornik municipality ..." and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we go, please, to the last page in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's signed by Mr. Vasilic, who was the person you met, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I comment?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you the question: Are you saying that all of that activity recorded there must have taken place after your inspection and before the end of June?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was saying that we called at Karakaj and Zvornik and that the police station wasn't really operational, that it was in two offices. Later on they moved to Zvornik to work. I know that on the occasion of our visit, which took about an hour too, there was a personnel problem --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, you told --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we were trying to persuade Vasilic to take over. He was deputy commander or assistant commander, as far as I remember. And before him Slavko Jelic was commander but he got killed. That was the problem. We were there only on a very short visit and they weren't in their own facilities. There were in new facilities in Karakaj and they really didn't do anything there. That's why I said that our first visit wasn't really an inspection. I only found a couple of people there. I remember that there was Petko and that there was Vasilic, who was deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... all right --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or -- anyway, he wasn't chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is what -- this is what I'm trying to ask you about: You're saying, effectively, because that's what you said to Mr. Cvijetic, page 21877, you went mid-May or late May to this Karakaj place, they were totally disorganised, they weren't operational, the police station didn't have executive personnel, there was Marinko Vasilic and Petko Panic. So everything they describe there on your account must have taken place between mid-May and the 29th of June when this report was sent up; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen this report nor did we conduct an inspection there. That's why I don't know about this report. We basically didn't do anything there. I can only say what I know. And I know about this information, that for a month or two this man stayed there, Pantelic. That is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. See, this is what I want to ask you about. I really am suggesting to you, Mr. Orasanin, that for whatever reason this visit or inspection was nothing of the sort, was it? Wasn't even beginning to be an inspection?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't disagree. The first visit was just to go and see what they had there, to make a snap-shot. But what we saw was total disorganisation. There weren't any police there. They were all frightened. It was the same at Skelani and Zvornik. They were very short visits. And we didn't even start with the instructive inspection. And that's the only truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you see, this isn't right, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I see the time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so we take the break, to pick this up in another 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We apologise for not having announced an extended break at the beginning, but we were in a meeting. We didn't think it would take as long as it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think it will come as a surprise to hear that I won't be finishing today, though I would've if all things had been equal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to stay with the subject of Zvornik and what you described as this non-working police station when you did your visit in May. Could you have a look, please, at a document which has been given the number 20159 at tab 1D of the Prosecution bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I say that it was disclosed in August of last year in connection with a witness who testified then. If we go, please, to -- does it say "Lists of SJB Workers" on the front? And can we go to the next page, please in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: A list --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- of public security station workers at Zvornik. SJB chief Milorad Lokancevic, I think that's the person you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then we see administration, communications, national security.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then can we go, please, to the next page both in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, only for the sake of the record, we repeat our usual objection that this document does not meet the conditions. It isn't on the 65 ter list. And it's for the Trial Chamber to rule on its admissibility. It was disclosed in connection with the Prosecution witness, but it was not used with that witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. And I'm dealing with his assertions, and this goes to his credibility as a witness. At that stage, of course, nobody knew that this witness was going to turn up and make these assertions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, next page, it's a letter dated the 1st of June, 1992, addressed to the Serbian contemporary municipal government, which is a somewhat odd translation, I think. I think it's the municipality. And it says, submissions of the workers engaged in SJB Zvornik. Enclosed with the file, we submit to you the list of active and reserve police at Zvornik Public Security Station being submitted according to the payment of salaries for the month of May. Do you agree, Mr. Orasanin, it appears that the SJB chief Mr. Pantelic is asking for the municipal authorities to pay the salaries?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that they were controlled by the Crisis Staff, but when I was on my visit, they were in Karakaj. This is from a later period. I'm speaking about the time when the police station was functioning in Karakaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, no, no, just wait. Because you said this was a non-functioning police station. Right, now, go to the next page, please. They're asking for the salaries of those who worked in May, so at the time when you made this visit. Employed SJB workers, numbers 1 to 33. Mr. Pantelic, Mr. Vasilic, Petko Pantic, the person you spoke to, and so on and so forth. 33 of them in all. Do you see?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we then go -- the rest are the reserve police. And it runs -- I'm not going to take you through all the pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you pull up the B/C/S for a moment, please, or is it the next page, maybe. Yes. Yep. Reserve police numbers 1 and, indeed, if we go to the last page, please, in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does that show that there are -- there were working or attached in May, and in fact it gives the dates that they apparently were working, some 187 reserve police?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, are you suggesting that Mr. Pantelic was trying to extort money from the municipality by giving totally false lists of police officers who were working? Surely not.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no. I didn't mean that. But possibly this list was compiled later. I had the feeling that in those three offices in Karakaj, I only found a few people on duty. That's how they functioned in that remote police facility. Later they moved to another location. Karakaj is 5 kilometres from Zvornik. That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but you gave the impression that you were told this was a non-functioning, non-working, non-staffed police station. And we've seen the report, Mr. Orasanin, that was done in June. We've now seen the list of police officers. Are you saying that Mr. Vasilic, who you spoke to, and Mr. Panic and everybody else told you this was a non-operating police station?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I had the feeling when I was there, because we were only there for an hour, I spoke to Marinko, I didn't even speak to Pantelic about anything, and that's why we weren't able to conduct an inspection. They had their premises inside a company in Karakaj at that period. I didn't see any people there. That's why I had this feeling. But I said that we were only there on a very brief visit. And possibly later when they moved to the police station building, once the conditions were created, possibly this list was compiled, but I didn't see this these people there on the premises. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you'd been sent -- I'm sorry, Mr. Orasanin, but presumably with some difficulty, given the conditions that undoubtedly existed in May, you and your fellow inspectors had been sent off to do an inspection. Now, why did you only spend one hour there and not make any inquiries, as you clearly didn't?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the first visit is something that I don't really consider an inspection because the legal obligations are very serious. When we went to Skelani, Zvornik, and Brcko, we didn't really review the lists or registers. They were only very short visits. But we left it for later inspections because we couldn't really do it. We only went there to see if there is anybody, and if they are properly staffed, whether there's a commander, a deputy, and that was our intention. And I believe that we were successful in this respect. But the police station was not in its own building, the building that was built to be a police station. They weren't at Zvornik at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've said that three times, Mr. Orasanin. What I am trying to get you to explain is how, given the reality of how Zvornik was operating, as we can see from documents, you gained the impressions it was not operating at all and presumably reported back to your superiors, or somebody else, that it wasn't operating.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the functioning is concerned, I meant the executives, the commander and his deputy. Slavko Eric, the deputy commander was killed as far as I know, and they said that their problem was nobody wanted to take over his duty. And that's what I remember, something conspicuous. But I didn't see any people there at that location. And that's why I concluded that they weren't functioning, because management was a problem. They had the staffing issue of nobody willing to accept the position of the one who was killed. That's what I remember. Marinko Vasilic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ask Mr. Vasilic, Do you have police officers or reserve police officers who are working at this time? Did you ask that simple question?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. There was Drago Borovcanin on behalf of the police administration. That was his duty. I was tasked to see about crime prevention. The police station should be placed under the command of the ministry, and he should become commander instead of the one who was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well, I think I've taken this as far as I can take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do ask that this document now be admitted. As I say, it was disclosed last year; that's accepted by the Defence. Its relevance has only become now apparent as a result of the evidence which this witness gave, and this document clearly demonstrates that this witness is in error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees that the document may be admitted and marked as being received on the issue of credibility only.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2351, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, although I'm going to turn to that a little later in more detail, you also asserted that this period, and indeed for some months, Zvornik was not attached to any CSB. Do you remember making that assertion?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that the stations in Podrinje were not included in the organisational structure. And later on they were placed under the responsibility of the Sarajevo CSB. I don't remember the date when that happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Could you have a look, please, at a document which is P -- it's actually an exhibit, I think. Just a moment, just let me check that. I don't want to get that wrong. It is P2005. Tab 4C. This is apparently a fax document, but it comes, apparently, from the chief of the CSB Bijeljina, Mr. Jesuric. Did you know Mr. Jesuric at the time to be the chief of the CSB in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is he actually writing to the ministry for the attention of the minister, stating that on the 27th of April, so before your visit: "I visited the Zvornik SJB, acquainted with him, learned about their situation. We have agreed upon steps for returning the situation back to normal and everyday life in Zvornik municipality. You will be informed on time about particular operation," blah, blah, blah, and "help forwarded from Bijeljina CSB to Zvornik SJB." So could you be wrong, Mr. Orasanin, when you say that Zvornik was not attached to any CSB?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know and as far as I can see, at the time the Bijeljina CSB did not function. It was later organised. And this document reads Bijeljina SJB, and it speaks about the Zvornik SJB. So it's the pre-war organisation and the war-time organisation. And as far as I know, the Bijeljina CSB was only set up later. And this document does not speak about the CSB. I think that's how it was. I remember, yes, there was a special station. The Zvornik SJB was under the Bijeljina CSB, during the war remained in the same position as before the war. I cannot see here that this is about the CSB. This is about SJBs. They kept the pre-war organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the English version, the line "Bijeljina SJB" is indeed missing, whereas it's present in the original. You can see it says "Stanica Javne Bezbjedrosti Bijeljina" in the third line from the top.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, you're quite right, but that's not --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not dealing with where -- it's the text. Does the text read, and if it doesn't, please let me know: "You will be informed about -- on time about particular operations, assignments, and help forwarded from Bijeljina CSB to Zvornik SJB"? Is that what the document says? And equally, is the signature of Mr. Jesuric, chief of Bijeljina CSB?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I remember that the two stations were functioning. Bijeljina is one and Zvornik is the other. This is probably a mistake. We should check the stamp. But as far as I remember -- actually, I'm sure that I remember that there was no Bijeljina CSB. It came into existence later when the MUP headquarters was moved to Bijeljina, possibly in July or August. I don't understand why Jesuric is writing to the station if they are at the same level. This must be a mistake, this -- where it says CSB. We should check the seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, the Court has heard evidence, firstly, and you've seen it, that the CSB Bijeljina was created by the Law on Internal Affairs passed in March 1992. Additionally, the Court has seen, and I can show it to you if we can find it, the appointment of Mr. Jesuric as the chief of the CSB made by Mico Stanisic in April, or temporary appointment, I think it was, until later. So please do not go off on frolics of your own. If the fact is that you simply don't know and are just guessing when you make these statements, then say so. Now, the original question was: You clearly, Mr. Orasanin, when you made these assertions about these stations and the CSBs, were unaware of what the situation was; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't know the organisation, although it was there. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'm reminded that the temporary appointment of Mr. Jesuric as the chief of the CSB Bijeljina is P2017. And it was confirmed on the 15th of May, as so many of the others were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, finally, on Zvornik, can we look at one other document to lay to rest all your -- the information you gave about Zvornik. Could you look, please, at P348, which is tab 35A. And it's a very long document, so I'll try and direct you to the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we get the document that Ms. Korner cited as the foundation for her assertion on the appointment of Mr. Jesuric. That was P2017. That's how it was recorded. Could we just see it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, it's the wrong exhibit number. It's 14 -- I'm sorry, P1409. Sorry, Your Honours, I gave the wrong number. It's P1409. Can we take off this document and go to that one, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the stamp and the signature of Mico Stanisic, 1st of April?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And does that show Predrag Jesuric temporarily appointed as head of the CSB Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to this document. But I don't remember this. I know that he was chief of an SJB. That's what I remember. I don't know this document. He was chief of an SJB. And when we were in Bijeljina, that's how we treated them. And we asked to see Boro Grkinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a convenient moment for the comparison of both documents. The one used by Ms. Korner --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry. This is cross-examination. If Mr. Cvijetic wants to take up these matters, he can do so in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just scroll up because there is a handwritten remark at the top. We can see a date, a handwritten date. It says sent to Bijeljina on 19 April 1992. And there's another appointment with the same date, and I call it up and Ms. Korner did erroneously. Maybe it would be good to see them both. P2017. One appointment --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really object to this. I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, do I understand the basis of your intervention to be that the document to which Ms. Korner has referred is the - I don't want to use the word wrong - is the wrong document, and that if the correct document is shown, she may wish to rephrase her question? Because if it isn't that, then I would have to agree with her that you should wait until your turn comes in re-examination. Could you clarify that for me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, I can, very briefly. I'm afraid that the Prosecutor is leading the witness astray because -- and that's why it would be good to see both documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, up till now there's never been any suggestion that Mr. Jesuric was not the chief of the CSB Bijeljina. We've got the permanent appointment as well, but I don't want to get sidetracked down this. I think if Mr. Cvijetic says I've got it wrong, then he can deal with it in re-examination. The permanent appointment is P546, the 15th of May. But, Your Honours, I only went down this because he said he wasn't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we leave it for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, can I just make it absolutely clear that there is another appointment the same day. I don't want anybody to think I'm misleading the Court. But his permanent appointment is confirmed on the 15th of May, and the evidence throughout from numerous witnesses has been that's what Mr. Jesuric was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the only point that I'm trying to make with you, Mr. Orasanin, is that you make sweeping assertions without really knowing the facts. That's the problem, isn't it? Mr. Orasanin? You actually make sweeping assertions when you're not aware of the facts?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Madam Prosecutor. As for this document, it's probably a valid document. But at the time I thought he was chief of the SJB because that's what he was before, and that's what I remembered. And probably this temporary point is valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I must intervene. The third document Ms. Korner has referred to is not an appointment -- is not the appointment of a chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can see that in order to satisfy -- I'm just going to be continually interrupted. Let's have all the three documents one, after the other, that refer to Mr. Jesuric. Could we have P2017 up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. On the 19th of April, so some 18 days later, Mr. Jesuric is also -- is temporarily appointed to the task and duties of the head of the personnel section in the MUP BiH. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this appointment either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally can we look at the one on the 15th of May, which is P456.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Decision: Predrag Jesuric is appointed as head of the CSB Bijeljina, member of the MUP staff Serbian Republic Bosnia and Herzegovina for command and control of the general forces of the Ministry of the Interior." Did you know about that, Mr. Orasanin?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about the decision. I know that he was physically present in Bijeljina in that building, but what kind of job he did, whether he was chief of SJB or a centre chief, but he always used the same office. I know that he was physically present, but the personnel -- the details of the personnel policy, well, I worked in a different administration, the crime prevention administration, and it wasn't my duty to be acquainted with these decisions except in my line of work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand. Mr. Orasanin, stop. I understand that. I'm not criticizing you for one moment for not knowing about these appointments. I'm merely pointing out to you, as I say, that when you made the assertion about Zvornik not having any -- being attached to any CSB from that document from Mr. Jesuric, who signs himself chief of the CSB, it would appear you were mistaken. But I've dealt with that. And I'd like now, if I can not have any further interruptions, please, to go back to the document I wanted to ask you about, which is P348 at tab 35A. Now, at line 2 of this handwriting document, can we see that it says report of the Serbian security centres in Zvornik for the year 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we go, please, in the English to page 20 of 59, it may be because of the -- the number -- the ERN -- it's quite difficult. Can I just see what comes up. In B/C/S I can say that the -- it should be 0176-9084. Yes, that's it in English. And in B/C/S it should be ... yep. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. It says it's a description of the activities undertaken on the organisation and winning over of personnel for the Serbian MUP by the 4th of April. And there's a long description, which I think the Court has already been through before, about how Zvornik was taken over.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But can we go, please, to the -- it will be three pages on in English, and it should be on page 1769086 [sic], page 19. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And here we go on Karakaj, Mr. Orasanin: "Serb SJB based in Karakaj was formed on the 5th of April, 1992. The station had about 29 active and 50 reserve policemen. A decision was then reached on the makeup of the senior staff SJB chief, the station was operational, had organised all patrols, held all check-points, barricades, and reserve had risen to 70 policemen. SJB personnel acting together with the forces of the Serb TO took hold of the town on the 8th of April." And then under C do you see, I hope, that "in addition, work on the clearing up of the SJB building continued so the building could be used -- the station in Karakaj transferred its operation to the building of Zvornik SJB sometime around the 15th of May." I hope that appears there somewhere. Can you see that bit?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, sorry, it's the wrong page. No, I'm sorry, Your Honours, I haven't got the right page in English. The page in English should say, at the bottom, 22 of 59. Next page, please. Oh, previous, sorry. It's so small I can't read it, myself, on the screen. For some unknown reason the translation or the copying was done in that way. It should be the penultimate paragraph on that page that's got C. Can we highlight that paragraph, please. Zoom in, rather. In English. No, you can't. See, it's going to be difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Anyhow, and finally: "During May, the following organisational units operated within the SJB: A police station of about 400 men strong, 31 of whom were policemen active service, crime enforcement department which had 7, department for general, legal, and administration affairs which had 9."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We need to go to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "At the end of May, the SJB had a total of 420 employees." Now, that's all I want to put to you about Zvornik. You must have been wrong, mustn't you, Mr. Orasanin, when you told the Court that this was a non-operating, non-functional police station?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is this: When we paid a visit to Karakaj, it was my impression that they were not functioning, because I only found three or four people there. That was what I saw. They were in Karakaj when I saw them. We were there in the first half of May, and this report speaks about a later time after they had changed their location and there were conditions in place for their work. When we visited Karakaj, they were not on their own, they shared the building with somebody else. They had one, maybe two or three, offices. That's why my impression was that they were not properly functioning, because I only found four or five of them there. And then they moved to Zvornik to a police station where the conditions were better, and the report is about that, about that second location, which was a big improvement, hence the difference in the impressions and descriptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Orasanin, could you remind me how long you were in Karakaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An hour. We just popped over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So as for Zvornik, your conclusion about the functioning of the SJB in Karakaj was based on a one-hour visit? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And is that a reasonable -- a reasonable way of concluding about how a police station functions, when you are there for one hour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree. Those were blitz visits. And that's why I was saying that they were not supervisions or inspections. There were no conditions in place for that. We visited those stations only in passing. And when we saw the conditions that they were in, we went back in order to report for things to be improved. That was the purpose of our visits to Bijeljina, Brcko. Those are not proper inspections as they were prescribed. What I saw is what I -- is the truth of the matter. This is the truth. That's what I saw. Later on things may have changed, but I know nothing about that. I'm talking about the first visit, about what we saw during that visit, and about information that we received on that occasion. We saw a few rooms -- sometime later their rooms had been broken -- were broken into. I learned that subsequently. But during that one hour that I was there, I just saw what I saw. It was not a proper inspection. I can't speak about anything that happened subsequently in Zvornik and Bijeljina. I based my impressions on our blitz visit, on that one hour. We could not do a professional inspection, and we couldn't do anything that was within our purview. My colleagues will confirm that, because later on they returned to their previous building, the building that was functioning properly, where all the conditions were in place for their functioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I would suggest that you move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. The difficulty, Your Honour, is -- [Microphone not activated] -- the difficulty is, of course, these are quite important, these inspections, but.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just answer this simply: Were your instructions from your superiors who sent the three of you out there simply to conduct, as you put it, a blitz visit?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When we departed, we were aware of all the regulations and the laws. We thought that we could -- we were able -- we would be able to do everything properly. When we arrived, we saw that there was a state of confusion, we saw that there were problems. That's why we --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, stop. All I asked you was whether your instructions were for blitz and you've answered that no. Right. Let's move, please, to Skelani, that same visit, where you told the Court, at page 2188 -- 21880, that you saw somebody there, and there was -- a Mr. Milanovic, and there wasn't a proper police station. Right. Skelani, would you agree, was a very, very small place indeed?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just trying to find my census document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I had flitting around somewhere the census document. I just wanted to put the ... All right, I'll come back to that. Well, can we have it up on the screen, actually, it's the easiest. It's P230, please. No, that's not -- is that P230? Sorry, then I've given the wrong, as usual. Oh, I'm sorry, P2321. And can we go in that to page -- we don't need any English for it. P2321. And I'd like to go to the ERN number which is 0048213 [sic]. Sorry, 8213. Your Honours, I don't want -- at the moment I'm afraid there's -- every now and again my note goes wrong. I did have the right pages printed out, but they've gone walk-about as well. So forget that. Page 303. All right. Instead of which, can we have, please, a document which is 20163, 16A. [Microphone not activated] This is tab 16A that we are looking at now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does that show that at this very small town, which we've found the census in a moment, in May this was apparently an operating SJB, with some ten officers working?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the list proves it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So again, Skelani, which, as I say -- well, perhaps we better show -- we finally found the census.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Can we have the document back I asked for, 2321, Exhibit P2321. And can we go in that to 0048-2139. Page 230, B/C/S. We only need it in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Number 2 on the list, Skelani, which is part of the Srebrenica municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 1948 through to 1981.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We need to go to the next page, please, to find out the figures for 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Second line down again, 1.123 in total persons, of which 950 were Muslim, 160 were Serb, and seven describe themselves as Yugoslav; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was in fact, wasn't it, largely a Muslim town which had been taken over by the Serbs, attacked, hadn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had never been in Skelani before that. That was my first time. And the information here, yes, this is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And therefore it had an adequately functioning SJB for the number of people who were present, didn't it, in May?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Previously it was just a brand [as interpreted] police station, if I remember the organisation well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Branch police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but -- I'm sorry, you gave the Court the impression again, Mr. Orasanin, that when you visited Skelani there was virtually nothing there, there was just one man. In fact, it had, did it not, a perfectly functioning police station; it had a chief, a station commander, and eight other police officers working there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that it was totally dysfunctional or not functioning. There were police officers there. But as far as I remember, they had problems. They were just -- there was just one office. I don't know whether they went on to develop into a proper police station and I don't know on whose orders. However, before we arrived there, the ministry had not done it. The ministry had not set it up properly. That's what I can claim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, didn't the witness answer this question at page 73 -- your question -- 72/24 and 25, your question, and 73, line 2: "Yes, the list proves it."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Sometimes, you know, you get caught up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's all I wanted to ask you there. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, in this particular case, although I would like to have it exhibited, it is not a document that had been disclosed before and that is because nobody had ever talked about Skelani, nor is Srebrenica one of the municipalities in the indictment, but until this witness came along and gave this information. So it's a document that purely goes to his credit. And I make the application notwithstanding that it hadn't been disclosed before because this really could not have been anticipated and equally wasn't relevant to any matter at all except, as I say, his credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Would you remind us the tab number, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's tab --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is it 16A?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, he has looked at the document and spoken to it. We don't need to have it exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I won't press the matter then. Your Honours, I'm going to move on to a slightly different topic, and I note -- well, I can start it and we'll see where we go in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You discussed -- sorry, you answered questions from Mr. Cvijetic, beginning at 21883, about the police officers not being under your command because you -- they hadn't got decisions as to the appointment from the minister, and we dealt with that briefly. But one of the things that you said, and this is at 21884, is: "Once an employee of the MUP receives a decision, then according to the regulations and according to the rules of procedure on internal structure, the person has certain rights, but also has certain obligations. The rights are that he would get a salary." So, Mr. Orasanin, if there are documents showing that persons were receiving salaries as police officers, then it follows from what you are saying whether or not there was a written appointment, it was accepted that he was a police officer?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know and as far as I know the regulations, it is clear. A person who had received decision on employment pursuant to the labour law and the law on internal affairs, that person has rights and obligations. And as far as the payrolls are concerned, those persons whose names are on the payrolls must use police authorities. That's why they are authorised officials, which is uniformed police who work on crime prevention and crime detection. And they had to use police authorities. Anybody else working in financial departments or administrative departments, they don't have police authorities, and they are not considered authorised personnel or authorised officials because they are not police officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. But this is the point. You -- your complaint, and many others have complained the same, is that appointments or people are being put into place not by the minister but by Crisis Staffs. It was open, wasn't it, to the minister to accept that appointment and agree with it, whether in writing or verbally?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that this is correct. That when a decision is issued, that a person acquires rights and obligations and is in a position to use police authorities. It is not whether they are on a payroll or whether they receive salaries, especially when it comes to the reserve police. According to regulations, when a policeman is engaged as a reserve policeman and if he only works for seven days, he is furnished with an official ID, a pistol, and that person performs duties for seven days, and during those seven days he is an authorised official. When his tour is finished, he returns all those things, goes home, and he no longer has authorities as a policemen. Those are the differences. And as far as I know, this is how things worked, this is how it was regulated. It doesn't mean that everybody on the payroll belonged to the MUP or that they were authorised officials. And I'm now referring to crime prevention and detection police officers and inspectors.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand the difference between those who were authorised officials and those who were not. What I'm asking you about, and just listen to this question: Even if the original appointment is done by the Crisis Staff or the municipal authority, it is open, is it not, to the minister to accept and authorise that appointment, whether in writing or verbally, or by simply doing nothing at all?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in -- what I know is that those people had to comply with certain requirements, irrespective of who issued the decision. That was the problem. They had to comply with certain legal requirements. And as for that decision that you're referring to, in this case it was the Crisis Staffs who appointed people. But they were not authorised to do that. Under the law, they were not supposed to have anything to do with the police organisation. Neither the local authorities nor the Crisis Staffs were supposed to have anything to do with the police. They should have acted in keeping with the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop, Mr. Orasanin. I understand that. What I am putting to you -- just try and concentrate and don't go off on a tangent. Is it, in your long experience as a police officer, open to the minister to accept and confirm, whether verbally or in writing, an appointment which has been made by the Crisis Staff? Is that within his authority, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR ORASANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could only issue decisions in keeping with the law. He could not have done it ad hoc. He could not have made ad hoc approvals. But this is not what I'm versed in. I'm not a legal expert or professional.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honours, that will be as far as we can take it today, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We reconvene in the afternoon tomorrow. And I'm advised that we are in this courtroom again. So we take the adjournment.
